messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The accident happened on a clear Tuesday afternoon, on a stretch of highway Leilani had driven a hundred times. A pickup truck crossed the median and struck her sedan head-on. She remembers the sound—a deep, metallic groan—and the sensation of the steering wheel pressing into her ribs. But when she tries to describe it now, she loses the thread. The words scatter. Some moments are brutally clear: the smell of hot asphalt, the way the windshield spiderwebbed. Others are blank, like someone erased a strip of film. Her memories come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, and that fragmentation has become its own source of dread.

In the months since, Leilani has come to believe she no longer belongs anywhere. She used to be a happy person, but now she is always miserable. Nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore. She is a professor of marine biology, and her lectures once felt like a calling; now she stands before her students and feels like a ghost performing a script. What frightens her most is the certainty that she has been permanently changed—that the woman who loved her work, her husband, her morning coffee on the porch, is gone. She is certain she will never get her back.

This sense of being hollowed out has made her hypervigilant in ways she cannot control. She wakes during the night to check whether she is safe, her hand reaching for the lamp before her brain catches up. During the day, she is superalert, watchful, on guard—scanning parking lots for trucks, flinching at the sound of a horn. She has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe, and that she must be ready at all times. This vigilance, in turn, deepens her sense of alienation. The more she watches for danger, the more she feels like a stranger in her own life.

The fragmented quality of her memory feeds directly into this cycle. When she tries to tell her husband what happened, she loses the thread and cannot finish, and this failure convinces her that she is broken beyond repair. The gaps in her memory feel like evidence that she has lost something essential about herself. And because she cannot hold the whole event in her mind, her brain fills the blanks with fear. She has begun to experience flashbacks—suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, her body pinned to the driver’s seat, her hands gripping an invisible wheel. These flashbacks are triggered by the most ordinary things. A car with a dented bumper. A discussion about accidents in the faculty lounge. Even the sight of a vehicle that has been hit makes her stomach drop.

These triggers have reshaped her daily life. She now avoids the highway entirely, taking back roads that add forty minutes to her commute. She has stopped attending department meetings where crash imagery might come up in casual conversation. She told her colleagues she was busy, but the isolation has cost her. Her husband has noticed she no longer wants to drive anywhere together. She has started to feel detached, unreal—a dissociative feeling that creeps in when she is most overwhelmed, as though she is watching herself from a distance.

The loops tighten. Her hypervigilance makes her more sensitive to triggers, and each trigger brings a flashback that fractures her memory further. Each fractured memory reinforces her belief that she is lost, and each moment of feeling lost makes her scan the world more desperately for threats. She wakes in the night to check if she is safe, and finds only the dark. She used to be a happy person. Now she is always miserable.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning last week when she could not bring herself to get out of the car in the university parking lot. She sat there for forty minutes, gripping the wheel, certain that if she stepped out, something terrible would happen. She called her husband from the driver’s seat, and he drove her home. She is afraid of what she is becoming. But she is more afraid that the woman she used to be is already gone, and that no amount of talking will bring her back.
